Scripted controllers can therefore run through the same\nservice a model would use:\n\n    from lightlag_controllers import REFERENCE, drive, make\n    from lightlag_mcp.client import connect\n\n    with connect(\"http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp\") as tools:\n        drive(tools, make(REFERENCE))\n\n`target` is a URL (Streamable HTTP), `StdioServerParameters`, or a server object\nfor in-process tests. Requires the `mcp` package, version 2.x.\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nimport asyncio\nimport concurrent.futures\nimport contextlib\nimport json\nimport threading\nfrom typing import Any, Dict, Iterator, List\n\nfrom mcp import Client\n\n\nclass RemoteToolError(ValueError):\n    \"\"\"The server rejected a call. A ValueError, like the simulator's own rejections.\"\"\"\n\n\nclass McpTools:\n    \"\"\"The five public methods, each a blocking MCP tool call.\"\"\"\n\n    def __init__(self, client: Client, loop: asyncio.AbstractEventLoop) -> None:\n        self._client = client\n        self._loop = loop\n\n    def _call(self, tool: str, arguments: Dict[str, Any]) -> Any:\n        future = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(self._client.call_tool(tool, arguments), self._loop)\n        result = future.result()\n        text = \"\".join(getattr(block, \"text\", \"\") for block in result.content)\n        if result.is_error:\n            raise RemoteToolError(text)\n        return json.loads(text)\n\n    def rules(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        return self._call(\"rules\", {})\n\n    def map(self) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        return self._call(\"map\", {})\n\n    def telemetry_log(self) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:\n        return self._call(\"telemetry_log\", {})\n\n    def uplink(self, commands: List[Dict[str, Any]]) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:\n        return self._call(\"uplink\", {\"commands\": commands})\n\n    def advance(self, ticks: int = 1) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n        return self._call(\"advance\", {\"ticks\": ticks})\n\n    def tool_names(self) -> List[str]:\n        future = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(self._client.list_tools(), self._loop)\n        return [tool.name for tool in future.result().tools]\n\n\n@contextlib.contextmanager\ndef connect(target: Any) -> Iterator[McpTools]:\n    \"\"\"Open an MCP session on a background event loop and yield blocking tools.\"\"\"\n    loop = asyncio.new_event_loop()\n    thread = threading.Thread(target=loop.run_forever, name=\"lightlag-mcp-client\", daemon=True)\n    thread.start()\n    ready: \"concurrent.futures.Future[Client]\" = concurrent.futures.Future()\n    stop_holder: List[asyncio.Event] = []\n\n    async def session() -> None:\n        # The session is opened and closed inside one task, as the SDK requires.\n        stop = asyncio.Event()\n        stop_holder.append(stop)\n        try:\n            async with Client(target) as client:\n                ready.set_result(client)\n                await stop.wait()\n        except BaseException as failure:\n            if not ready.done():\n                ready.set_exception(failure)\n                return\n            raise\n\n    running = asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe(session(), loop)\n    try:\n        client = ready.result(timeout=30)\n        try:\n            yield McpTools(client, loop)\n        finally:\n            loop.call_soon_threadsafe(stop_holder[0].set)\n            running.result(timeout=30)\n    finally:\n        loop.call_soon_threadsafe(loop.stop)\n        thread.join(timeout=5)\n        loop.close()","lineStart":1,"lineEnd":102,"totalLines":102,"truncated":false}},"title":"app/lightlag_client.py","time":{"start":1794709633028,"end":1794709633039}},"metadata":{"google":{"thoughtSignature":""}},"id":"prt_1dd07b7fe001uRyGrCQDoYx11J","sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","messageID":"msg_1dd078fba001xUL7641Cqi150t"}}

applied.\n6: Standard library only, Python 3.9+.\n7: \"\"\"\n8: \n9: from __future__ import annotations\n10: \n11: import math\n12: from typing import Any, Dict, List, Optional, Sequence, Tuple\n13: \n14: TERRAIN_CODES = {\"b\": \"bedrock\", \"r\": \"regolith\", \"s\": \"sand\", \"k\": \"rocks\"}\n15: \n16: # Published physics. `rules()` returns this table unchanged.\n17: PHYSICS: Dict[str, Any] = {\n18:     \"segment_m\": 0.25,                  # a drive is integrated in steps of this many wheel metres\n19:     \"max_tilt\": 0.36,                   # rise over run (about 20 degrees); steeper ground stops the rover\n20:     \"slip_base_ranges\": {\"bedrock\": [0.01, 0.05], \"regolith\": [0.05, 0.12],\n21:                          \"sand\": [0.15, 0.35], \"rocks\": [0.12, 0.24]},\n22:     \"slip_grade_gain\": {\"bedrock\": 0.8, \"regolith\": 1.5, \"sand\": 3.5, \"rocks\": 1.2},\n23:     \"slip_noise\": 0.02,                 # one uniform draw in +-this per executed drive\n24:     \"slip_max\": 0.95,\n25:     \"side_slip_gain\": {\"bedrock\": 0.1, \"regolith\": 0.3, \"sand\": 0.8, \"rocks\": 0.2},\n26:     \"drive_cost_per_wheel_m\": {\"bedrock\": 0.30, \"regolith\": 0.36, \"sand\": 0.50, \"rocks\": 0.60},\n27:     \"climb_cost_per_m\": 2.0,            # energy per metre of height gained; descending returns nothing\n28: }\n29: \n30: \n31: class Surface:\n32:     \"\"\"A height grid with bilinear interpolation, and one terrain class per grid cell.\n33: \n34:     `elevation_cm[j][i]` is the height in centimetres at x = i * cell, y = j * cell.\n35:     `terrain[j][i]` is the class code of the cell with that vertex as its south-west corner.\n36:     \"\"\"\n37: \n38:     def __init__(self, cell: float, elevation_cm: Sequence[Sequence[int]], terrain: Sequence[str]) -> None:\n39:         self.cell = float(cell)\n40:         self.h: List[List[float]] = [[value / 100.0 for value in row] for row in elevation_cm]\n41:         self.ny, self.nx = len(self.h), len(self.h[0])\n42:         if self.ny < 2 or self.nx < 2 or any(len(row) != self.nx for row in self.h):\n43:             raise ValueError(\"the elevation grid must be rectangular, at least 2 by 2\")\n44:         if len(terrain) != self.ny - 1 or any(len(row) != self.nx - 1 for row in terrain):\n45:             raise ValueError(\"terrain needs one code per grid cell\")\n46:         self.codes: List[str] = [str(row) for row in terrain]\n47:         self.width = (self.nx - 1) * self.cell\n48:         self.height = (self.ny - 1) * self.cell\n49: \n50:     def inside(self, x: float, y: float) -> bool:\n51:         return 0.0 <= x <= self.width and 0.0 <= y <= self.height\n52: \n53:     def locate(self, x: float, y: float) -> Tuple[int, int, float, float]:\n54:         \"\"\"The cell (i, j) holding the point and the point's fractions inside it.\"\"\"\n55:         fx, fy = x / self.cell, y / self.cell\n56:         i = min(self.nx - 2, max(0, int(fx)))\n57:         j = min(self.ny - 2, max(0, int(fy)))\n58:         return i, j, fx - i, fy - j\n59: \n60:     def sample(self, x: float, y: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float, str]:\n61:         \"\"\"Height, d(height)/dx, d(height)/dy and terrain code at a point.\"\"\"\n62:         cell = self.cell\n63:         fx, fy = x / cell, y / cell\n64:         i = min(self.nx - 2, max(0, int(fx)))\n65:         j = min(self.ny - 2, max(0, int(fy)))\n66:         tx, ty = fx - i, fy - j\n67:         low, high = self.h[j], self.h[j + 1]\n68:         h00, h10, h01, h11 = low[i], low[i + 1], high[i], high[i + 1]\n69:         height = (h00 * (1 - tx) + h10 * tx) * (1 - ty) + (h01 * (1 - tx) + h11 * tx) * ty\n70:         gx = ((h10 - h00) * (1 - ty) + (h11 - h01) * ty) / cell\n71:         gy = ((h01 - h00) * (1 - tx) + (h11 - h10) * tx) / cell\n72:         return height, gx, gy, self.codes[j][i]\n73: \n74:     def elevation(self, x: float, y: float) -> float:\n75:         return self.sample(x, y)[0]\n76: \n77:     def slope(self, x: float, y: float) -> float:\n78:         _, gx, gy, _ = self.sample(x, y)\n79:         return math.hypot(gx, gy)\n80: \n81:     def terrain(self, x: float, y: float) -> str:\n82:         return TERRAIN_CODES[self.sample(x, y)[3]]\n83: \n84:     def cell_max_slope(self, i: int, j: int) -> float:\n85:         \"\"\"The steepest slope anywhere in cell (i, j). On a bilinear patch that is at a corner.\"\"\"\n86:         low, high, cell = self.h[j], self.h[j + 1], self.cell\n87:         h00, h10, h01, h11 = low[i], low[i + 1], high[i], high[i + 1]\n88:         south, north = (h10 - h00) / cell, (h11 - h01) / cell\n89:         west, east = (h01 - h00) / cell, (h11 - h10) / cell\n90:         return max(math.hypot(south, west), math.hypot(south, east),\n91:                    math.hypot(north, west), math.hypot(north, east))\n92: \n93: \n94: def drive(surface: Surface, physics: Dict[str, Any], x: float, y: float, heading_deg: float, metres: float,\n95:           slip_base: Dict[str, float], noise: float = 0.0, battery: Optional[float] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n96:     \"\"\"One drive command: `metres` of wheel travel at `heading_deg` from (x, y).\n97: \n98:     Per step of `segment_m` wheel metres, with the ground sampled where the step starts:\n99:       grade  = slope along the heading (rise over run), cross = slope to the left of it\n100:       slip   = clip(slip_base[terrain] + slip_grade_gain[terrain] * max(0, grade) + noise, 0, slip_max)\n101:       the rover moves segment * (1 - slip) along the heading and\n102:       segment * side_slip_gain[terrain] * cross to the right (downhill across the heading)\n103:       energy = segment * drive_cost_per_wheel_m[terrain] + climb_cost_per_m * max(0, height gained)\n104:     The step is refused, and the drive ends, if it would leave the map (`stop` = \"map_boundary\")\n105:     or end on ground steeper than `max_tilt` (`stop` = \"tilt\"). With a `battery`, the drive also\n106:     ends when the battery is spent (`stop` = \"battery\").\n107: \n108:     Returns the end position, wheel and ground metres, the energy used and `stop` (None if the\n109:     whole command ran).\n110:     \"\"\"\n111:     radians = math.radians(heading_deg)\n112:     ux, uy = math.cos(radians), math.sin(radians)\n113:     segment_full = physics[\"segment_m\"]\n114:     gain, side, cost = physics[\"slip_grade_gain\"], physics[\"side_slip_gain\"], physics[\"drive_cost_per_wheel_m\"]\n115:     climb, slip_max, max_tilt = physics[\"climb_cost_per_m\"], physics[\"slip_max\"], physics[\"max_tilt\"]\n116:     width, height = surface.width, surface.height\n117:     remaining = float(metres)\n118:     wheel = ground = energy = 0.0\n119:     stop = None\n120:     here, gx, gy, code = surface.sample(x, y)\n121:     while remaining > 1e-9:\n122:         segment = min(segment_full, remaining)\n123:         name = TERRAIN_CODES[code]\n124:         grade = gx * ux + gy * uy\n125:         cross = -gx * uy + gy * ux\n126:         slip = slip_base[name] + gain[name] * (grade if grade > 0 else 0.0) + noise\n127:         slip = 0.0 if slip < 0 else (slip_max if slip > slip_max else slip)\n128:         forward = segment * (1.0 - slip)\n129:         sideways = segment * side[name] * cross\n130:         next_x = x + ux * forward + uy * sideways\n131:         next_y = y + uy * forward - ux * sideways\n132:         if not (0.0 <= next_x <= width and 0.0 <= next_y <= height):\n133:             stop = \"map_boundary\"\n134:             break\n135:         there, next_gx, next_gy, next_code = surface.sample(next_x, next_y)\n136:         if math.hypot(next_gx, next_gy) > max_tilt:\n137:             stop = \"tilt\"\n138:             break\n139:         spent = segment * cost[name] + climb * (there - here if there > here else 0.0)\n140:         if battery is not None and spent >= battery - energy:\n141:             energy = battery\n142:             wheel += segment\n143:             ground += math.hypot(next_x - x, next_y - y)\n144:             x, y = next_x, next_y\n145:             stop = \"battery\"\n146:             break\n147:         energy += spent\n148:         wheel += segment\n149:         ground += math.hypot(next_x - x, next_y - y)\n150:         remaining -= segment\n151:         x, y, here, gx, gy, code = next_x, next_y, there, next_gx, next_gy, next_code\n152:     return {\"x\": x, \"y\": y, \"wheel\": wheel, \"ground\": ground, \"energy\": energy, \"stop\": stop}\n\n(End of file - 2, max(0, int(fy)))\n        tx, ty = fx - i, fy - j\n        low, high = self.h[j], self.h[j + 1]\n        h00, h10, h01, h11 = low[i], low[i + 1], high[i], high[i + 1]\n        height = (h00 * (1 - tx) + h10 * tx) * (1 - ty) + (h01 * (1 - tx) + h11 * tx) * ty\n        gx = ((h10 - h00) * (1 - ty) + (h11 - h01) * ty) / cell\n        gy = ((h01 - h00) * (1 - tx) + (h11 - h10) * tx) / cell\n        return height, gx, gy, self.codes[j][i]\n\n    def elevation(self, x: float, y: float) -> float:\n        return self.sample(x, y)[0]\n\n    def slope(self, x: float, y: float) -> float:\n        _, gx, gy, _ = self.sample(x, y)\n        return math.hypot(gx, gy)\n\n    def terrain(self, x: float, y: float) -> str:\n        return TERRAIN_CODES[self.sample(x, y)[3]]\n\n    def cell_max_slope(self, i: int, j: int) -> float:\n        \"\"\"The steepest slope anywhere in cell (i, j). On a bilinear patch that is at a corner.\"\"\"\n        low, high, cell = self.h[j], self.h[j + 1], self.cell\n        h00, h10, h01, h11 = low[i], low[i + 1], high[i], high[i + 1]\n        south, north = (h10 - h00) / cell, (h11 - h01) / cell\n        west, east = (h01 - h00) / cell, (h11 - h10) / cell\n        return max(math.hypot(south, west), math.hypot(south, east),\n                   math.hypot(north, west), math.hypot(north, east))\n\n\ndef drive(surface: Surface, physics: Dict[str, Any], x: float, y: float, heading_deg: float, metres: float,\n          slip_base: Dict[str, float], noise: float = 0.0, battery: Optional[float] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]:\n    \"\"\"One drive command: `metres` of wheel travel at `heading_deg` from (x, y).\n\n    Per step of `segment_m` wheel metres, with the ground sampled where the step starts:\n      grade  = slope along the heading (rise over run), cross = slope to the left of it\n      slip   = clip(slip_base[terrain] + slip_grade_gain[terrain] * max(0, grade) + noise, 0, slip_max)\n      the rover moves segment * (1 - slip) along the heading and\n      segment * side_slip_gain[terrain] * cross to the right (downhill across the heading)\n      energy = segment * drive_cost_per_wheel_m[terrain] + climb_cost_per_m * max(0, height gained)\n    The step is refused, and the drive ends, if it would leave the map (`stop` = \"map_boundary\")\n    or end on ground steeper than `max_tilt` (`stop` = \"tilt\"). With a `battery`, the drive also\n    ends when the battery is spent (`stop` = \"battery\").\n\n    Returns the end position, wheel and ground metres, the energy used and `stop` (None if the\n    whole command ran).\n    \"\"\"\n    radians = math.radians(heading_deg)\n    ux, uy = math.cos(radians), math.sin(radians)\n    segment_full = physics[\"segment_m\"]\n    gain, side, cost = physics[\"slip_grade_gain\"], physics[\"side_slip_gain\"], physics[\"drive_cost_per_wheel_m\"]\n    climb, slip_max, max_tilt = physics[\"climb_cost_per_m\"], physics[\"slip_max\"], physics[\"max_tilt\"]\n    width, height = surface.width, surface.height\n    remaining = float(metres)\n    wheel = ground = energy = 0.0\n    stop = None\n    here, gx, gy, code = surface.sample(x, y)\n    while remaining > 1e-9:\n        segment = min(segment_full, remaining)\n        name = TERRAIN_CODES[code]\n        grade = gx * ux + gy * uy\n        cross = -gx * uy + gy * ux\n        slip = slip_base[name] + gain[name] * (grade if grade > 0 else 0.0) + noise\n        slip = 0.0 if slip < 0 else (slip_max if slip > slip_max else slip)\n        forward = segment * (1.0 - slip)\n        sideways = segment * side[name] * cross\n        next_x = x + ux * forward + uy * sideways\n        next_y = y + uy * forward - ux * sideways\n        if not (0.0 <= next_x <= width and 0.0 <= next_y <= height):\n            stop = \"map_boundary\"\n            break\n        there, next_gx, next_gy, next_code = surface.sample(next_x, next_y)\n        if math.hypot(next_gx, next_gy) > max_tilt:\n            stop = \"tilt\"\n            break\n        spent = segment * cost[name] + climb * (there - here if there > here else 0.0)\n        if battery is not None and spent >= battery - energy:\n            energy = battery\n            wheel += segment\n            ground += math.hypot(next_x - x, next_y - y)\n            x, y = next_x, next_y\n            stop = \"battery\"\n            break\n        energy += spent\n        wheel += segment\n        ground += math.hypot(next_x - x, next_y - y)\n        remaining -= segment\n        x, y, here, gx, gy, code = next_x, next_y, there, next_gx, next_gy, next_code\n    return {\"x\": x, \"y\": y, \"wheel\": wheel, \"ground\": ground, \"energy\": energy, \"stop\": stop}","lineStart":1,"lineEnd":152,"totalLines":152,"truncated":false}},"title":"app/lightlag_surface.py","time":{"start":1794709633281,"end":1794709633293}},"id":"prt_1dd07b8fd001RYM42fP4Ka2BQP","sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","messageID":"msg_1dd078fba001xUL7641Cqi150t"}}

Such a\ntool typically waits until everything the command started has let go of its output, and when\nthe limit is reached it stops the whole process group. A program started with `&` or `nohup`\nis still in that group, and in a form like `cd /app && nohup python3 autopilot.py > log 2>&1 &`\nthe shell that waits for it still holds the tool's output. The call then hangs until the limit\nand the program is killed with it, in the middle of a campaign that does not wait.\n\nA program started here has its own session and no link to the caller's input or output: it\nreads from nowhere and writes to the log file, unbuffered so the log is current. Standard\nlibrary only; needs a POSIX system.\n\"\"\"\n\nfrom __future__ import annotations\n\nimport argparse\nimport os\nimport subprocess\nimport sys\nfrom typing import Optional, Sequence\n\n\ndef start(command: Sequence[str], log: str = \"autopilot.log\") -> int:\n    \"\"\"Start `command` detached, appending its output to `log`; return its process id.\"\"\"\n    environment = dict(os.environ, PYTHONUNBUFFERED=\"1\")\n    with open(log, \"ab\") as stream:\n        process = subprocess.Popen(list(command), stdin=subprocess.DEVNULL, stdout=stream,\n                                   stderr=subprocess.STDOUT, start_new_session=True,\n                                   close_fds=True, env=environment)\n    return process.pid\n\n\ndef main(argv: Optional[Sequence[str]] = None) -> int:\n    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(\n        description=\"Start a program that keeps running after this command returns.\",\n        usage=\"python3 detach.py [--log FILE] command [argument ...]\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"--log\", default=\"autopilot.log\", help=\"file the program's output is appended to\")\n    parser.add_argument(\"command\", nargs=argparse.REMAINDER, help=\"the program and its arguments\")\n    args = parser.parse_args(argv)\n    command = args.command[1:] if args.command[:1] == [\"--\"] else args.command\n    if not command:\n        parser.error(\"give the program to start, for example: python3 autopilot.py\")\n    try:\n        pid = start(command, args.log)\n    except OSError as failure:\n        print(\"could not start {}: {}\".format(command[0], failure), file=sys.stderr)\n        return 1\n    print(\"started pid {}; its output goes to {}; stop it with: kill {}\".format(\n        pid, os.path.abspath(args.log), pid))\n    return 0\n\n\nif __name__ == \"__main__\":\n    sys.exit(main())","lineStart":1,"lineEnd":61,"totalLines":61,"truncated":false}},"title":"app/detach.py","time":{"start":1794709633286,"end":1794709633297}},"id":"prt_1dd07b902001leV1LsuHL9eOda","sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","messageID":"msg_1dd078fba001xUL7641Cqi150t"}}

It seems distance from base directly correlates with target worth, with near targets being worth 1.0, and further targets up to 5.0. Also, the `target_radius` and `base_radius` are 2.5m and 4.0m respectively, and failing to return to base within this radius by the end of the mission, or hitting a battery value of 0, will severely impact the score!\n\n\n**Calculating Solar Gain**\n\nI'm now focusing on battery dynamics. I've broken down the solar charging formula, considering the impact of efficiency and the sinusoidal nature of solar input over 420 ticks. Even with the minimum efficiency of 0.8, the average solar energy gain is approximately 1.57 per tick, but this fluctuates with the time of day! I'm also comparing this solar gain with energy expenditure.\n\n\n**Assessing Energy Expenditure**\n\nI'm now analyzing energy expenditure more precisely, especially considering terrain and the `climb_cost_per_m`. Drive costs are 2.50 units per 5m on sand, and 3.00 units on rocks. Climbing adds 2.0 per meter. Sampling costs 2.0. Solar charge fluctuates, ranging from approximately 700 to 850 over 420 ticks, with an initial 100-unit battery. Crucially, solar gain is lower than drive cost, especially at the mission's start and end, implying a risk of battery drain! Thankfully, I can use the exact battery charge from the very first telemetry packet!\n\n\n**Unveiling Battery Dynamics**\n\nI've just figured out the exact battery recharge/discharge order of operations! Solar charging happens first, capped at battery capacity. Then, the idle cost is subtracted. Lastly, the command's energy cost is deducted. This means that until the rover is actively draining battery below capacity, solar charging is capped, and efficiency is difficult to calculate! However, once the battery drops below its maximum, I can estimate the exact efficiency using the first uncapped solar tick. This provides a direct path to determining efficiency with extreme precision!\n\n\n**Determining Efficiency Dynamics**\n\nI've realized that I can pinpoint the *exact* `solar_efficiency` as soon as the battery isn't fully charged, around tick 5. I will estimate `0.9` before that, or a conservative value of `0.85` if I prefer. I'm focusing on the battery's behavior and the timing of its charging to refine these calculations. I'm also examining the code for calculating slip for drive commands.\n\n**Confirming Telemetry Accuracy**\n\nI've just had a major realization! The battery level, terrain class, and tilt values reported in each telemetry packet are *exact*, not estimates! This is a game-changer because I now have precise data on energy expenditure, terrain, and slope, allowing for highly accurate energy expenditure calculations.\n\n\n**Estimating Heading Bias**\n\nI'm now integrating the heading bias model. I've realized `visual_odometry` gives us `1 - slip`, and can be used to estimate `slip_base[terrain]` precisely online. I'm focusing on incorporating a Kalman filter (or perhaps an Extended Kalman Filter, or even a Particle Filter) to estimate both the rover's true position and the current `heading_bias` using the telemetry data. This should allow for much more accurate planning!\n\n\n**Quantifying Error Margins**\n\nI'm now calculating the error margins for my state estimates. Given the telemetry data's precision and the deterministic nature of rover motion, with only about 0.12m of uncertainty per step, I believe our estimates for position, heading bias, and slip_base can be incredibly accurate, perhaps even sub-meter, using a filter! The noise in the measurements (GPS, visual odometry, and so on) will become the limiting factor, and our filter choice, probably a form of Kalman filter, will be vital!\n\n\n**Refining Positional Precision**\n\nI've just been analyzing the impact of telemetry delay on positional accuracy. After accounting for a three-tick delay and propagating the state forward, it seems that our positional uncertainty at the moment the new command executes is around ~0.45 meters. Given this high level of accuracy, the rover can sample targets and return to base within their respective radii nearly always!\n\n\n","time":{"start":1794709720315,"end":1794709760194}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1794711119250,"sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","part":{"id":"prt_1dd1e2a48001cN1evqSlbhUSTR","messageID":"msg_1dd1e0dfe001vWRjbj3kCe1y8Q","sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","type":"reasoning","text":"**Analyzing Slowdowns Persistently**\n\nI've pinpointed a major bottleneck: in the `play_one_mission` function, the `planner.find_waypoints` method is called repeatedly within each tick. This happens whenever `d_target` is above 1.35, and it's called a whopping 420 times per seed. This frequent re-computation is the likely culprit for the significant delay when processing 3 seeds.\n\n\n**Caching Waypoints Strategically**\n\nI've realized a huge inefficiency: `planner.find_waypoints` is recalculating the same path repeatedly for a given target. Specifically, the method is re-computing the waypoints for the current target on every single tick, even though the rover is driving toward the same one. The solution is clear: cache the `current_wps` for each target ID (`tid`). This means the method will only call `planner.find_waypoints` the first time a target becomes active, and then we will simply follow the cached waypoints.\n\n\n**Optimizing Waypoint Strategy**\n\nI've got it! Now, whenever I reach a waypoint or the path to it is clear, I can shortcut straight to the next waypoint by popping `current_wps[0]`. This drastically reduces calls to `planner.find_waypoints`, slashing them from 420 per mission to a mere 25! It makes a huge difference; the total time drops from 21 seconds to 1.2 seconds!\n\n\n**Caching Dijkstra Results**\n\nI've been working on further optimizations! I'm now caching the results of Dijkstra's algorithm. By caching the `ticks_arr` and `en_arr` for each node (`u_node`), I'm significantly reducing recomputation.  This means that when a new target appears, I only need to run Dijkstra once for that new node and I can efficiently re-use existing Dijkstra calculations for existing targets.  This reduces the matrix build time significantly, from 1.8 seconds down to a mere 0.04!\n\n\n","time":{"start":1794711104072,"end":1794711119247}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1794711346073,"sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","part":{"id":"prt_1dd2139c5001aRTX4J2dOpppRQ","messageID":"msg_1dd20f6490017uOO8gs4QK0r0Q","sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","type":"reasoning","text":"**Analyzing Key Insights**\n\nI've just uncovered three critical insights from the local simulation tests using Seed 1, Seed 2, and Seed 3. The output has been eye-opening, and I need to delve into these revelations. I'm focusing on why a sample missed on tick 50. This initial observation points to something significant, and I need to fully understand its implications.\n\n\n**Investigating Missing Sample**\n\nI'm now zeroing in on why the sample at tick 47 from Seed 1 was missed. The key seems to be the re-adding of `t32`. The logs reveal that the rover had already queued a sample action for tick 47 at tick 43, yet it was not present in the replanned sequence at tick 44. I'm looking into the timing of discoveries d2 and d3, and the conditions around `compute_drive_command` at tick 42, specifically the distances that triggered either a drive or sample command.\n\n\n**Refining Sample Acquisition**\n\nI've been examining the critical missed sample at tick 47 and have a plan. The errors in `est_x` and `est_y` plus the offset are clear contributors to this missed sample. This caused a loss of 8 ticks and 16 battery units when the rover had to reverse course. To remedy this, I am tightening the sample acquisition criteria to ensure a near-perfect position. I will set `offset` to 0.35m and require `d_target <= 1.05 m`. This adjustment should prevent future sample misses.\n\n\n**Examining Battery Depletion**\n\nI'm now investigating the battery depletion scenario in Seed 1, specifically why the rover reached an `end_battery` of 3.69 and had a replanning event at tick 330. I've noted the planned sequence at tick 227 and the battery level drop during the rover's traversal. I'm focusing on the `eval_seq` function within `plan_tour` and how it handles the return-to-base leg when the battery is critically low, and how to improve that.\n\nI'm also considering the implications of the rover's position estimation error. With a `2.0 m` margin within a `target_radius = 2.5 m`, I am quite confident there won't be a sample miss.\n\n\n**Addressing Battery Drain**\n\nI'm now investigating the reasons behind the discrepancies in battery depletion. I see that the calculated `dh` only considers the height difference between grid cells, ignoring smaller undulations, side-slip corrections, heading noise, and stop/start overhead. These omissions lead to underestimation of energy expenditure in the plan. My focus now is on incorporating these factors to create a more realistic battery model. I'll need to re-evaluate how the `TerrainPlanner` computes energy costs to improve plan accuracy.\n\n\n**Verifying Energy Consumption**\n\nI've confirmed the underestimation of energy and time by analyzing Seed 1. The model's prediction of 11% less energy and 6% fewer ticks directly led to replanning and the near-depletion of the battery. I'm validating the impact of those variables. The actual spent energy was higher than predicted. Now, I will re-examine `t_mat` and `e_mat` to align them with reality.\n\n\n**Validating Model Predictions**\n\nI've made a breakthrough! Adjusting `t_mat` to include a `1.05x + 0.35` factor and `e_mat` to incorporate `1.12x + 0.6` yields a significantly more accurate model. My predictions now align with the rover's performance within 1-2%, preventing over-commitment and ensuring all targets are sampled. I'm also examining why `plan_tour` failed to include `t34` in the planned sequence at tick 330, even though it was near the Base.\n\n\n**Clarifying Empty Sequence Issues**\n\nI've just pinpointed the root cause of the empty sequence issue: `eval_seq([])` returning `-1.0` at Tick 330. I see that the sequence at Base when `bat` is at 10.0, the return leg `dt = t_mat[cur][0]`, after arriving at Base, if `bat` was `< min_bat - 2.0` and `solar[ntk]` after Tick 380 is small, waiting couldn't bring `bat` back up before `max_tick = 409`, thus returning -1.0 for every sequence.\n\n\n\n**Implementing Battery Adjustment**\n\nI've discovered a critical flaw in the battery management logic. The strict `min_bat = 14.0` requirement throughout the mission caused the planner to reject sequences, even those containing the final targets on the return path, because they couldn't meet the target battery threshold. To address this, I'm implementing a dynamic `min_bat` value. During the mission (`tk < 350`), it will be 14.0. At the end (`tk >= 350`), only 9.0 is needed. This will allow the rover to sample on the return to base, which may improve the output. {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1794711667861,"sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","part":{"id":"prt_1dd2653eb001GBaowuTn4ioDov","messageID":"msg_1dd263bb1001lgcq640brxWK3l","sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","type":"reasoning","text":"**Analyzing Battery Levels**\n\nI'm focusing on the `end_battery` values across different seeds within a specific run. I've noticed a significant variance: 84.88, 77.03, and 99.85. My immediate question is, why are these values so different? It's especially puzzling considering the rover returned to base and idled for an extended period, so the variance isn't just about runtime.\n\n\n**Investigating Rover Idle Time**\n\nI'm now digging into why the rover idled at the base for so long (ticks 370-420) despite nearby targets. It looks like the change to the `tk_adj` calculation introduced a significant overestimate of the tour's duration (+30 phantom ticks), leading the planner to believe the rover was much closer to its deadline. Also, there's a problem with replanning. I've found that the rover didn't trigger `need_replan = True` when `planned_seq` became empty at tick ~350, so it didn't revisit the map for nearby targets even though it had 70 ticks left at the time!\n\n\n**Clarifying Time Calculation Error**\n\nI've pinpointed a major timing bug related to `t_mat`. The `math.ceil()` function, when combined with the prior calculation `raw_t * 1.045 + 0.25`, led to significant double-counting of time. It appears the initial ceiling operation alone added roughly 3% of the total time! This, in combination with later calculations, caused phantom time to be added. I'm focusing on the effect these calculation inaccuracies had on idle time for the rover. {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1794712100727,"sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","part":{"id":"prt_1dd2cd6bd001TRMwsibOpF1eyd","messageID":"msg_1dd2cad2b001MSsI0D3ZIzXmgf","sessionID":"ses_e22f8729dffeQ7FxVcBQtdw2Qr","type":"reasoning","text":"**Investigating a Discrepancy**\n\nI've hit a snag. Seed 1 in the run shows the agent ending with a battery level of 6.509, yet it's marked as not alive. I'm digging into why this happened. There was a safety stop detected shortly before the agent's demise. I'm retracing the execution steps. It's unclear how these two facts are compatible, so I'm investigating.\n\n\n**Unraveling Battery Depletion**\n\nI've determined the root cause: at tick 411, the agent was given a drive command despite a critically low predicted battery level, leading to immediate battery depletion and death. The logic allowed this drive command to be issued. The solar energy continued to add charge up to 6.509 even after the agent was dead. I'm now verifying the fix in the logic.\n\n\n**Analyzing the Parameter Shift**\n\nOkay, the root cause is now clear. I've pinpointed that the parameter shift dramatically impacted battery management. The updated formulas for `e_mat` and `tk_adj` led to an underestimation of energy and time, causing over-commitment and eventual battery depletion. The simulator just saved us. I'm now comparing the outcomes of the two runs to further analyze the effects of these formulas on energy calculations.\n\n\n**Synthesizing Test Lessons**\n\nI've distilled two crucial insights. First, the success of `tk_adj` and `e_mat` with adjusted coefficients is clear: on a bumpy surface, energy expenditure is approximately 11% higher than anticipated based on cell-center elevations, and the time adjustments accurately reflect real-world navigation. Second, I need a 'Hard Battery Survival Guard': allowing a command to drain the battery to zero results in a catastrophic score of zero.\n\n\n**Refining Safety Protocols**\n\nI'm now implementing a critical safety measure. No \"drive\" or \"sample\" commands are permissible if the predicted battery (`pred_bat`) could fall below 5.0. Moreover, I'm extending this protection: I will command \"wait\" if `pred_bat` is below 6.5, regardless of remaining ticks. If it's between 6.5 and 10, I'll scale down drives to avoid battery depletion. I'm also adding an \"Energy Return-to-Base Override\".\n\n\n**Implementing Return Safeguards**\n\nI've just added a critical override mechanism. I'm using precomputed energy requirements to return to base, and incorporating net solar energy forecasts for the remaining mission. The \"Energy Return-to-Base Override\" is triggered if the total available energy isn't enough to complete one more target visit and return, or if there's insufficient energy to get home safely. I'm considering scenarios for immediate base return.\n\n\n**Prioritizing Energy Over Time**\n\nI'm now fully committed to the \"Energy Return-to-Base Override.\" The example clarified a crucial point. While considering ticks remaining is important, focusing solely on time can be fatal when energy is depleted, particularly during sunset. I've integrated checks for energy sufficiency at every tick, not just at specific time thresholds, ensuring the rover can always return.\n\n\n**Validating the Energy Model**\n\nI'm now verifying the \"straight to base\" calculation. The key is confirming `pred_bat + rem_net_solar - e_ret` as the projected final battery level. The total energy gain from solar and cost of idleness from the current tick to the final tick will be invariant. The drive energy to the base will be `e_ret`. Therefore, if the projected battery is less than 13, I can safely initiate a return.\n\n\n**Confirming Energetic Return**\n\nI'm now putting the \"straight to base\" calculation to the test with realistic time and energy calculations. I'm focusing on validating the core assumption: the final battery level can be accurately predicted as `pred_bat + rem_net_solar - (e_to_T + 2.0 + e_T_to_Base)`. If I can guarantee this, and if the projection reveals insufficient energy for a Target visit, a direct return to base becomes my priority. The simulations should confirm this exact energy conservation guard in action!\n\n\n","time":{"start":1794712065725,"end":1794712100725}}}
